questions.question: Dana walks to work through snow and buys a warm coat for that walk. A month later she buys a second coat in a fashionable new colour. How should the two coats be classed?
options: It depends only on which coat cost more
Both are needs, since coats are clothing
The first is a need and the second is a want
Both are wants, since she could wear a jacket
questions.correctAnswer: The first is a need and the second is a want
questions.explanation: The same kind of item can be a need or a want depending on what it does for you. A coat for a cold walk to work is a need. A second coat bought for its colour is a want.

source.quote: A warm coat for a cold walk to work is a need. A second coat in this season's colour is a want. The same item moves across the line depending on what it does for you.

questions.question: Leo lives on a fixed amount each month. He signs up for streaming services and a gym first, then finds he cannot cover his electricity bill. Which change to his process fixes the problem?
options: Pick cheaper wants first, then pay needs from whatever remains
Pay for housing and other needs first, then pick wants from what remains
Pay half of every bill and half of every want each month
Drop all wants for good, since spending on them is a bad habit
questions.correctAnswer: Pay for housing and other needs first, then pick wants from what remains
questions.explanation: Needs come off the top, and wants get whatever is left. Wants are not bad in themselves. What matters is the order.

source.quote: The order is the lesson. The things you must pay come off the top. The things you would like get whatever remains.

questions.question: Why should someone record how they spend money now before deciding what to change?
options: Tracking raises income, which gives the plan more to work with
Recording spending is itself a budget, so no plan is needed after
Tracking shows which needs to skip so the month costs less
A plan built on guesses misses where money goes and soon fails
questions.correctAnswer: A plan built on guesses misses where money goes and soon fails
questions.explanation: You have to find where the money actually goes before you can fix it. A plan based on guesses breaks down quickly.

source.quote: You cannot fix a leak you have not found. A plan built on guesses will fail in the first week.

questions.question: Picture a month's money as a bathtub: income is the tap, each expense is a drain, and what stays in the tub at month's end can be saved. Why can that picture mislead someone whose month balances on paper?
options: Small daily purchases are too minor to count as drains
Income arrives only after all bills are paid, so saving must come first
Expenses always exceed income, so the tub never holds anything
Pay arrives in lumps on set days, so earlier bills can drain the account mid-month
questions.correctAnswer: Pay arrives in lumps on set days, so earlier bills can drain the account mid-month
questions.explanation: The picture assumes money flows in and out smoothly. In real life paychecks and bills arrive on different days, so you can run short partway through a month that balances overall.

source.quote: The picture breaks on timing, because a real paycheck arrives in lumps on set days while many bills leave on other days, so the tub can run dry mid-month even when the month as a whole balances.

questions.question: Priya's spending plan has no room for a gaming chair she wants but does not need. The chair goes on sale at 40 percent off. What should she do?
options: Buy it and cut that month's grocery money to cover it
Skip it, since a cheaper want is still unplanned spending on a want
Buy it, since a discount turns the purchase into saving
Buy it only if the sale is about to end
questions.correctAnswer: Skip it, since a cheaper want is still unplanned spending on a want
questions.explanation: A discount does not turn a want into a need or make it part of the plan. The spending plan decides, not the price tag.

source.quote: A bargain on a want is still spending on a want. The plan, not the price tag, decides.

sets.title: Chapter 2: A cushion for bad days

questions.question: Why should a household treat a surprise bill as something to plan for, rather than as bad luck?
options: They are rare, but each one is too large for savings to cover
They mostly hit households that never made a monthly budget
Most adults meet one in a normal year, so a plan should expect it
They are usually small enough to pay from the next paycheck
questions.correctAnswer: Most adults meet one in a normal year, so a plan should expect it
questions.explanation: More than half of adults face an unexpected expense in a typical year. That makes it a normal event to prepare for, not a rare misfortune.

source.quote: It is not bad luck that happens to someone else. In a normal year, more than half of adults meet one.

questions.question: Maya has $800 set aside as an emergency cushion. Her phone still works, but a newer model is on sale for $300. What should she do with the cushion?
options: Use it, as long as she refills it from next month's leftover money
Use half, since only a full three-month fund has to stay untouched
Leave it alone, since a wanted upgrade is not an emergency expense
Use it, since a sale price is a surprise she could not have planned
questions.correctAnswer: Leave it alone, since a wanted upgrade is not an emergency expense
questions.explanation: The cushion is kept only for unplanned emergencies such as repairs, medical bills or lost income. A new phone is a choice, not an emergency.

source.quote: It is money specifically set aside for unplanned expenses or financial emergencies, such as car repairs, home repairs, medical bills or a loss of income. It is not money for a holiday or a new phone.

questions.question: Picture emergency savings as a cushion that catches you when a bill knocks you over. In what way does that picture fail, and what habit does the failure point to?
questions.explanation: A real cushion keeps its size, but savings shrink each time they pay a bill. They must be rebuilt to protect against the next shock.

source.quote: a real cushion stays the same size after you fall on it, but this one gets thinner every time it catches you, until you fill it back up.

rubric.point: Unlike a real cushion, savings get smaller each time they are used to pay a bill.
rubric.quote: but this one gets thinner every time it catches you, until you fill it back up

rubric.point: So after using it, you should build it back up.
rubric.quote: as you need to use some of your emergency savings, build it up again.

rubric.point: A cushion that is never refilled will not protect against the next shock.
rubric.quote: A cushion that caught one fall and was never refilled will not catch the next.

questions.modelAnswer: A real cushion stays the same size, but savings get thinner every time they pay a bill. So you have to refill them after each use, or they won't be there for the next shock.

questions.question: Two households each face a $600 car repair. One pays from savings and the other takes out a loan. Why does the repair end up costing the second household more?
options: Borrowing adds its own price on top, so the one-time bill grows
The repair itself gets pricier because a loan delays the work
Repair shops charge higher rates to customers who pay with a loan
The household paying from savings gets a discount for paying in cash
questions.correctAnswer: Borrowing adds its own price on top, so the one-time bill grows
questions.explanation: The extra cost comes from the price of borrowing, not from the repair itself. Savings pay the bill at its real size.

source.quote: If a surprise is paid by borrowing, the one-time emergency expense may grow significantly larger than the original bill. That extra cost is the price of borrowing

questions.question: Someone wants an emergency fund but feels overwhelmed by a goal of three months of expenses. Why does it make sense to start with a fund of a few hundred dollars instead?
questions.explanation: A small fund is within reach and matches the shocks people meet most often. The larger fund for lost income can come later.

source.quote: Most people build the small one first, because it is reachable and because the repair bill is the shock they meet most often.

rubric.point: A small fund is a reachable goal.
rubric.quote: Most people build the small one first, because it is reachable and because the repair bill is the shock they meet most often.

rubric.point: Repair-type bills are the most common shocks, and a modest sum covers many of them.
rubric.quote: Setting aside $500 to $1,000 can cover many unexpected expenses.

rubric.point: The larger fund serves a different, rarer shock: months without a paycheck.
rubric.quote: The large one carries a household through months without a paycheck.

questions.modelAnswer: A few hundred dollars is reachable, and it covers the shocks people meet most often, like a car or appliance repair. The bigger three-month fund is for a rarer event, losing your income, and can be built later.

sets.title: Chapter 3: Banks, credit unions and deposit insurance

questions.question: Why is a bank able to pay interest on the money people keep in their accounts?
options: It lends depositors' money out and earns from that lending
It earns returns on items kept in its safe deposit boxes
It charges a storage fee on the bills held in its vault
The federal insurer pays it a fee for each insured account
questions.correctAnswer: It lends depositors' money out and earns from that lending
questions.explanation: Deposits go into a pool the bank lends from. Borrowers pay the bank to use that money, and that lets the bank pay depositors a little.

source.quote: The bank can pay you because it puts your money to work. Banks accept deposits and lend money

questions.question: Maria is building an emergency fund to cover a sudden car repair. Which place suits that money best?
options: A certificate of deposit, because it pays the highest interest
Her everyday checking account, so it is mixed with spending money
A savings account, reachable quickly and kept apart from spending
An investment sold at her bank, since the bank itself is insured
questions.correctAnswer: A savings account, reachable quickly and kept apart from spending
questions.explanation: A cushion must be ready the day something breaks. A savings account can be reached in a day, earns a little, and stays separate from spending money. A certificate of deposit penalizes early withdrawal.
questions.concept: where to keep an emergency cushion

source.quote: You can reach it in a day, it grows a little, and it sits apart from the checking account you spend from.

questions.question: A certificate of deposit usually earns more than a savings account. What does the saver give up in return?
options: The right to hold more than one account at that bank
Any interest at all until the full term has ended
Free access to the money for a set time, or some interest is lost
Federal insurance on the money while it is locked away
questions.correctAnswer: Free access to the money for a set time, or some interest is lost
questions.explanation: The higher rate is payment for agreeing to leave the money alone. Withdrawing early usually costs some of the interest earned. Certificates of deposit are still covered by deposit insurance.

source.quote: In exchange, you agree to leave the money alone for a set time. Take it out early and you will likely lose some of the interest you earned.

questions.question: Dana has $150,000 in checking and $150,000 in savings, both in her name alone, at one insured bank. If the bank fails, how much of her money is insured?
questions.explanation: Accounts in one person's name alone at the same bank fall in the same ownership category. Their balances are added together and share a single $250,000 limit.

source.quote: You are insured up to $250,000 for the combined balance of the two, not for each.

questions.question: Someone pictures deposit insurance as a seat belt built into every insured account: if the bank crashes, the belt holds you. What does that picture get right, and where does it mislead?
questions.explanation: The picture captures the reliable protection when a bank fails. It misses the dollar limit and the fact that non-deposits are never covered.

source.quote: a seat belt protects whatever is in the seat, but this one stops at a dollar limit and does nothing at all for things that were never deposits.

rubric.point: It gets right that insured depositors are reliably protected when a bank fails.
rubric.quote: If the bank crashes, the belt holds you, and it has held every insured depositor since it was fitted.

rubric.point: It misleads because the protection stops at a dollar limit.
rubric.quote: The FDIC covers at least $250,000 per depositor, per ownership category, at each insured bank.

rubric.point: It misleads because things that are not deposits, such as investments, get no protection at all.
rubric.quote: Things sold as investments are not deposits, and they are not insured even when you buy them from an insured bank.

questions.modelAnswer: It gets right that insured deposits are reliably protected if the bank fails; no insured depositor has lost money. But a seat belt protects everything in the seat, while deposit insurance stops at $250,000 per category per bank and covers nothing that isn't a deposit, like investments.

sets.title: Chapter 4: Credit, debt and your credit report

questions.question: Lee makes the smallest required payment on a credit card every month without fail. Does that put Lee on a set schedule to become debt-free?
options: No; the card must instead be repaid in full within one year
No; the account stays in good standing, but the debt itself remains
Yes; the card company stops charging interest once payments begin
Yes; regular payments clear any card debt within a fixed term
questions.correctAnswer: No; the account stays in good standing, but the debt itself remains
questions.explanation: Paying the minimum keeps you current, but there is no fixed repayment date and the debt does not go away.
questions.concept: minimum payment does not end debt

source.quote: There is no fixed time to repay a card as long as you make the minimum payment each month. It does not make the debt go away.

questions.question: Dana is choosing between two credit cards. One has a lower interest rate but extra yearly charges. The other has a higher interest rate and no extra charges. Which single figure best compares what borrowing on each card costs?
options: The minimum payment each card would require every month
The credit limit, since a higher limit means cheaper borrowing
The yearly rate that folds the interest and other charges together
The interest rate alone, since charges are separate from borrowing
questions.correctAnswer: The yearly rate that folds the interest and other charges together
questions.explanation: The APR combines the interest rate and the card's other charges into one yearly cost of borrowing, so it is the figure to compare.

source.quote: Card companies add the interest rate and the card's other charges together into that one figure. The APR is the cost of borrowing money over a year.

questions.question: Mia's card has no grace period. Why does paying part of her balance on the 5th of the month, rather than the 25th, lower her interest?
options: Interest is charged once at month's end on the highest balance
Interest is figured each day, so fewer days unpaid means less interest
Card companies grant a discount as a reward for paying early
Early payments lower the yearly rate the card quotes next year
questions.correctAnswer: Interest is figured each day, so fewer days unpaid means less interest
questions.explanation: Interest builds up day by day on the balance, so money paid sooner stops costing interest sooner.

source.quote: Without a grace period, timing still matters. Because interest builds up day by day, paying some or all of the balance sooner means paying less interest.

questions.question: Why can a large card balance take years or even decades to clear when only the smallest required payment is made each month, and what shortens that time?
questions.explanation: Interest keeps being added each month, so a small payment barely reduces the balance. Paying more breaks that loop.

source.quote: With high balances, it can take years, even decades, to pay a card off that way. Each month, interest is added to what you owe.

rubric.point: Interest is added to the balance every month.
rubric.quote: Each month, interest is added to what you owe.

rubric.point: A small payment barely moves the balance because the new interest eats most of it.
rubric.quote: Because each month interest is added to what you owe, so a small payment barely moves the balance.

rubric.point: Paying more than the minimum clears the card faster and costs less in total.
rubric.quote: A borrower who pays more than the minimum each month pays the card off in less time, and pays less in total.

questions.modelAnswer: Each month new interest is added to what you owe, so a small payment barely shrinks the balance and the debt drags on. Paying more than the minimum pays it off faster and lowers the total cost.

questions.question: Why can one person have several different credit scores at the same time?
questions.explanation: A score is computed by a formula from reported data, so a different formula, different data, or a different day gives a different number.

source.quote: Each score depends on the data used, the scoring model, the source of the data and even the day it was calculated.

rubric.point: A score is calculated by a formula (scoring model) from the information in a report.
rubric.quote: Companies use a mathematical formula, called a scoring model, to build the score from the information in your report.

rubric.point: Different data, sources, models, or calculation dates produce different scores.
rubric.quote: Each score depends on the data used, the scoring model, the source of the data and even the day it was calculated.

rubric.point: The underlying data can differ because creditors don't report to every bureau.
rubric.quote: Creditors are not required to report to every one of these companies.

questions.modelAnswer: A score is a number a formula computes from whatever data a report holds. Different scoring models, different bureaus' data, or even a different calculation day give different results.

questions.question: Two accounts each start with $1,000 at the same yearly rate, and nobody adds money to either. By year five, one account is earning more interest each year than the other. What explains the difference?
options: Its rate quietly rises each year as the balance gets older
Its balance is federally insured, which adds a yearly bonus
Its earlier interest stayed in the account and now earns interest too
It pays interest only on the first deposit, so it is safer
questions.correctAnswer: Its earlier interest stayed in the account and now earns interest too
questions.explanation: With compounding, past interest joins the balance, so each year's interest is paid on a bigger base. The other account pays only on the original deposit.

source.quote: With compound interest, you earn interest on the money you save and on the interest that money earns.

questions.question: At the same yearly rate, $1,000 under simple interest and $1,000 under compound interest are close after ten years but far apart after thirty. Why does most of the gap open up in the later years?
options: Compounding only starts once the original deposit has fully doubled
Compounding works on a base that keeps growing, so each year's gain beats the last
The compound rate itself climbs over time, while the simple rate stays fixed
Simple interest stops paying anything once the first decade is over
questions.correctAnswer: Compounding works on a base that keeps growing, so each year's gain beats the last
questions.explanation: A larger balance earns a larger amount of interest at the same rate. Compound growth therefore speeds up the longer it runs. The rate itself never changes.

source.quote: A small ball picks up a thin layer of snow, and a bigger ball picks up a thicker layer, so it grows faster the bigger it gets.

questions.question: Ana and Ben each make one equal deposit at the same assumed rate, compounded yearly. Ana leaves hers for 30 years. Ben starts ten years later and leaves his for 20. Why does Ana end up far more than one-third ahead of Ben?
questions.explanation: Compound growth is uneven over time. Ana's extra decade comes at the end, when her balance is largest and earns the most.

source.quote: That is why time matters so much: the last decade does more work than the first.

rubric.point: Interest is added to the balance and then earns interest itself.
rubric.quote: Interest from last year joins the pile, and this year it earns interest too.

rubric.point: Growth is small early and piles up in the later years.
rubric.quote: The early years look almost the same, and the difference piles up at the end.

rubric.point: Ana's extra decade is a late, high-growth decade, so it adds far more than an early decade would.
rubric.quote: That is why time matters so much: the last decade does more work than the first.

questions.modelAnswer: Compounding pays interest on earlier interest, so growth speeds up the longer money sits. Ana's extra ten years are the final ones, when her pile is biggest and earns the most, so they add far more than ten early years would.

questions.question: Someone saves $100 a month for 30 years, $36,000 in all, at an assumed 5% compounded monthly, and ends with $83,226. What does this show about where the final balance came from?
options: The extra is guaranteed, because monthly saving removes the risk
Most of the balance is still the money they deposited themselves
Growth exactly matched deposits, so every dollar simply doubled
Most of the balance is growth rather than money they put in
questions.correctAnswer: Most of the balance is growth rather than money they put in
questions.explanation: Of the $83,226, only $36,000 was deposited. The remaining $47,226, more than half, is growth.

source.quote: Of that, $36,000 is the deposits themselves and $47,226 is growth. More than half the final pile is money the saver never put in.

questions.question: One investor puts all their savings into the stock market at a peak just before a crash. Another keeps adding money steadily through the low years that follow. Why does the second investor tend to do better, and what general rule follows?
questions.explanation: Putting everything in at one moment risks buying at the top. Steady adding buys at lower prices too, so consistency matters more than picking a start date.

source.quote: Steady saving matters more than a clever start date. Time in beats timing.

rubric.point: Money put in all at once at a peak can take decades to recover.
rubric.quote: people who put all their money into the market at its 1929 peak, before the crash, waited over 20 years for it to return to the same level.

rubric.point: Steady adders buy at lower prices during the slump, which leads to gains.
rubric.quote: those that kept adding money to the market throughout that time would have done very well for themselves, as the lower cost of stocks in the 1930s made for some hefty gains

rubric.point: The rule is to add money consistently over long periods rather than try to time the start.
rubric.quote: Steady saving matters more than a clever start date. Time in beats timing.

questions.modelAnswer: Putting everything in at a peak can mean waiting decades just to break even. Someone who keeps adding money buys cheaply during the slump and gains later. The rule is that steady saving over a long time beats trying to pick the perfect moment.

sets.title: Chapter 6: Stocks, bonds and funds: what an index fund and an ETF are

questions.question: A company goes bankrupt. Ana holds its bonds, Ben holds its preferred stock, and Cara holds its common stock. Who is paid first?
options: Cara, the common stockholder
All three are paid at once
Ben, the preferred stockholder
Ana, the bondholder
questions.correctAnswer: Ana, the bondholder
questions.explanation: In a bankruptcy, bondholders are paid before anyone else. Preferred stockholders come next, and common stockholders get whatever is left.

source.quote: When a company goes bankrupt, its bondholders are paid first and holders of preferred stock next. A common stockholder gets whatever is left, which may be nothing.

questions.question: An investor needs cash and sells her bond three years before it comes due. What can she expect to receive for it?
options: Exactly the full principal she originally lent
An amount that may be above or below its face value
Only the interest the bond has paid so far
The face value plus all the remaining interest
questions.correctAnswer: An amount that may be above or below its face value
questions.explanation: The full principal is only guaranteed back if the bond is held until it comes due. Sold early, its price can be higher or lower than face value.

source.quote: Sold before it comes due, a bond may be worth more or less than its face value.

questions.question: An investor places an order for mutual fund shares at 11 a.m. on a weekday. What price will she pay per share?
options: The net asset value from the previous day
The exchange price at the moment of her order
The next net asset value the fund calculates
Whatever price another investor will accept
questions.correctAnswer: The next net asset value the fund calculates
questions.explanation: Mutual fund shares are bought from the fund itself at the next calculated NAV. They are not traded on an exchange or with other investors.

source.quote: When the value of a fund's holdings rises, after its costs and debts are taken out, its NAV rises too. A mutual fund share is bought at the next calculated NAV.

questions.question: Why does an index fund usually cost less to hold than an actively managed fund?
options: It trades less because it only follows its index
A government agency insures it, so it carries less risk
It buys its shares in large blocks straight from the fund
Its manager's skill lets it beat the market more often
questions.correctAnswer: It trades less because it only follows its index
questions.explanation: A passive fund just holds what is in its index. That means less trading, lower taxes on gains, and lower costs than active management.

source.quote: Passive management usually means less trading, lower taxes on gains, and lower costs than active management.

questions.question: Two index funds hold the same companies. One gives bigger companies a bigger share, and the other gives every company the same share. Why might their returns differ?
questions.explanation: How an index is weighted decides how much each company's results count toward the whole, so the same companies can produce different returns.

source.quote: Another kind gives every company an equal place, and the two can return very different amounts.

rubric.point: In a size-weighted index, the largest companies make up much more of the fund, so their results dominate.
rubric.quote: In one common kind, the largest companies make up a much larger share of the list than the smallest ones.

rubric.point: In an equal-weighted index, each company counts the same, so small companies matter more and the returns can differ a lot.
rubric.quote: Another kind gives every company an equal place, and the two can return very different amounts.

questions.modelAnswer: In the size-weighted fund, the biggest companies make up most of the fund, so their results drive the return. In the equal-weighted fund, every company counts the same, so if smaller companies do better or worse than the big ones, the two funds can end up with very different returns.

questions.question: A company goes bankrupt and its assets are sold to pay its investors. Which group is paid last?
options: Every investor is paid an equal share
Holders of its preferred stock
Holders of its bonds
Holders of its common stock
questions.correctAnswer: Holders of its common stock
questions.explanation: Bondholders are paid first and preferred stockholders next. Common stockholders get only what is left, which may be nothing.

source.quote: A common stockholder gets whatever is left, and that may be nothing. Owning a share means standing at the back of the line.

questions.question: You own a bond that pays 3% a year. You want to sell it two years before it matures, but new bonds now pay 5%. What is likely to happen?
options: Buyers will pay extra for it because it is older
You may have to sell it below its face value
You will receive exactly its face value at the sale
You are not allowed to sell it until it matures
questions.correctAnswer: You may have to sell it below its face value
questions.explanation: When rates rise, newer bonds pay more. An older bond with a lower rate is less attractive, so you may have to sell it at a discount before maturity.

source.quote: When rates rise, newer bonds pay more, so an older bond with a lower rate may have to be sold at a discount.

questions.question: Why does spreading money across different kinds of assets reduce risk, instead of just averaging out the losses?
questions.explanation: Diversification works because asset classes do not all fall together. The conditions that hurt one asset class can help another.

source.quote: It works because different kinds of assets do not all fall at once. Conditions that make one asset class do poorly may improve returns for another.

rubric.point: Different kinds of assets do not all drop at the same time.
rubric.quote: It works because different kinds of assets do not all fall at once.

rubric.point: The conditions that hurt one asset class may help another.
rubric.quote: Conditions that make one asset class do poorly may improve returns for another.

rubric.point: Gains or steady value in some holdings can make up for losses in others.
rubric.quote: The hope is that if one investment loses money, the others make up for those losses.

questions.modelAnswer: Different kinds of assets do not all fall at once, and the conditions that hurt one can actually help another. So when one investment loses money, others may hold steady or rise and make up for the loss.

questions.question: Your plan was 60% stocks, but market gains have pushed stocks up to 80% of your portfolio. Which action brings the portfolio back to your plan?
options: Buy more stocks while their prices keep rising
Sell some stocks and put the money into bonds
Keep the new mix, since gains have lowered the risk
Sell some bonds and use the money to buy stocks
questions.correctAnswer: Sell some stocks and put the money into bonds
questions.explanation: Rebalancing means cutting back on the group that grew too large and adding to the other asset categories, so the original mix is restored.

source.quote: To get back to your mix, you may need to sell some stocks or add money to other asset categories.

questions.question: Why might a mutual fund investor never receive a bill for the fund's yearly operating costs?
options: A government agency covers the running costs
The seller pays them out of the sales load
The costs are taken out of the fund's assets
Funds charge these costs only when you sell
questions.correctAnswer: The costs are taken out of the fund's assets
questions.explanation: The fund deducts its expenses from its NAV, so investors pay them indirectly without writing a check. The costs are still listed in the prospectus.

source.quote: These costs are taken out of the fund's assets, which lowers your return. Funds deduct fees and expenses from NAV, so you pay them without ever writing a check.

sets.title: Chapter 8: Accounts and taxes: 401(k), IRA and Roth

questions.question: What happens to the income tax on money you put into a traditional 401(k) from your paycheck?
options: It is paid only on the earnings and never on the deposits
It is paid later, when the money comes out in retirement
It is paid now, and the withdrawals later are tax-free
It is cancelled for good as a reward for saving
questions.correctAnswer: It is paid later, when the money comes out in retirement
questions.explanation: The chapter says the 401(k) does not skip the tax. It moves it from the year you earn the money to the year you take it out and spend it.

source.quote: So the tax is not skipped. It is moved, from the year you earn the money to the year you spend it.

questions.question: Why can putting off the tax on retirement savings leave you with more money?
options: Deferred savings are taxed only on deposits, never on their growth
The tax rate on retirement withdrawals is fixed below today's rate
Money not paid in tax now stays invested and earns its own returns
The IRS adds matching money to accounts that delay their taxes
questions.correctAnswer: Money not paid in tax now stays invested and earns its own returns
questions.explanation: The advantage comes from compounding. The amount that would have gone to tax stays in the account and grows for decades. Whether you end up ahead still depends on your future tax rate, which nobody knows for certain.

source.quote: Money that would have gone to tax this year stays in the account instead, and it earns returns of its own for decades.

questions.question: A 52-year-old worker wants to put the most allowed into a 401(k) in 2027. What is the most they can put in?
questions.explanation: For 2027 the base limit is $25,500. Workers aged 50 and older can put in up to $34,000 that year.

source.quote: Workers 50 and older could put in up to $34,000 a year starting in 2027.

questions.question: In 2026, a 40-year-old with plenty of taxable pay puts $5,000 into a traditional IRA and $5,000 into a Roth IRA. What problem has this caused, and how can they fix it?
questions.explanation: Both IRAs count toward a single $7,500 limit, so this person has put in $2,500 too much. The excess is taxed every year it stays in the account.

source.quote: The same combined limit covers every Roth and traditional IRA you own, so opening a second account does not double it.

rubric.point: The $7,500 limit for 2026 covers both IRAs together, so $10,000 is $2,500 over the limit.
rubric.quote: For 2026, the total you put into all of your traditional and Roth IRAs together can be no more than $7,500

rubric.point: The excess is taxed at 6% for every year it stays in the IRA.
rubric.quote: Excess contributions are taxed at 6% per year for each year the extra stays in the IRA.

rubric.point: To fix it, they take the excess and its earnings back out by the due date of their tax return.
rubric.quote: The way out is to take the excess and its earnings back out by your tax return's due date.

questions.modelAnswer: They have gone $2,500 over the 2026 limit, because $7,500 is the total for all their IRAs combined, and that excess is taxed 6% every year it stays in the account. They should take the extra $2,500, plus anything it earned, back out by their tax return's due date.

questions.question: A neighbor tells you about a fund that he says pays 20 percent a year and cannot lose money. How should you treat this pitch?
options: As a good deal worth checking, since high returns usually mean low risk
As safe enough if the neighbor has already made money from the fund
As a sign of a scam, since anyone claiming little or no risk is a scammer
As acceptable if you invest only a small amount at first to test it
questions.correctAnswer: As a sign of a scam, since anyone claiming little or no risk is a scammer
questions.explanation: Every investment carries risk, and high returns come with high risks. The FTC rule in the chapter says that anyone who claims little or no risk is a scammer.

source.quote: The Federal Trade Commission's rule is that anyone who claims an investment has little or no risk, or will pay without much time and effort, is a scammer.

questions.question: Why does a scammer gain so much by telling you an offer will be gone tomorrow?
questions.explanation: The rush removes your time to check the offer, and checking is what protects you. A real offer would still be there later.

source.quote: Notice what the rush does. It takes away the one thing that protects you, which is time to check.

rubric.point: The rush takes away your time to check the offer, which is your main protection.
rubric.quote: It takes away the one thing that protects you, which is time to check.

rubric.point: Pressure such as limited space or a special deal is meant to make you skip research.
rubric.quote: They may say space is limited, or that you are getting a special deal, so that you skip the research.

rubric.point: A real investment can wait. A fake one needs your answer before you ask anyone else.
rubric.quote: A real investment will still be there next week. A fake one needs your answer before you ask anyone else.

questions.modelAnswer: The deadline takes away your time to check the offer, research it, or ask someone else, and that time is what protects you. A real investment would still be there next week, so a fake one has to get your answer fast.

questions.question: You get a text that claims to be from the SEC. It says your account has a problem and gives a link to fix it. What should you do?
options: Reach the agency yourself through its official phone number or website
Call the phone number listed in the text to talk to a real person
Click the link but enter only your name, not your account number
Reply to the text and ask the sender to prove who they are
questions.correctAnswer: Reach the agency yourself through its official phone number or website
questions.explanation: Scammers pose as trusted bodies, even the SEC. The fix is to cut the line and contact the agency through its official number or website, not through anything the message gives you.

source.quote: Contact the bank, company or agency through its official phone number or website, and ask whether there is a real problem.

questions.question: In a slow-building scam, why would a fraudster let you take out a small amount of money before asking for more?
questions.explanation: The small payout looks like proof that the scheme is real. That builds trust, so you will put in larger sums later.

source.quote: The small withdrawal is the hook, and it works because it looks like proof.

rubric.point: The scammer first builds trust, for example by posing as a friend or claiming the contact was an accident.
rubric.quote: Fraudsters may reach out on social media or by text, pretend to be an old friend, or claim they contacted you by accident.

rubric.point: The withdrawal works as a hook because it looks like proof that the profits are real.
rubric.quote: The small withdrawal is the hook, and it works because it looks like proof.

rubric.point: Once you trust it, they ask you to invest larger sums.
rubric.quote: Then they make it look as if you have profited, and may even let you withdraw a small amount. After that they ask you to invest larger sums.

questions.modelAnswer: Getting a little money back makes the scheme look real, so it works like proof and wins your trust. Once you trust it, the scammer asks you to put in much larger sums.

questions.question: In a pump-and-dump scheme involving a new coin, what happens to the people who bought because of the social media hype?
options: They lose most of their money after the promoters sell
They get their money back once the coin is officially registered
They profit as long as they buy before the promoters do
They gain slowly because the price keeps rising after the hype
questions.correctAnswer: They lose most of their money after the promoters sell
questions.explanation: The promoters push the price up, sell before the hype ends, and then the price falls quickly. Everyone else who bought loses most of their money.

source.quote: Then they sell before the hype ends. Then the price falls quickly, and everyone else who bought loses most of their money.

sets.title: Chapter 11: A first sum of savings, walked through

questions.question: How can one repair bill keep costing money long after it is paid?
options: It goes on a card or loan, where interest and fees keep adding to it
It is paid from savings, which then stop earning any interest at all
Its cost gets spread across many paychecks by automatic transfers
It forces investments to be sold, which locks in a large tax bill
questions.correctAnswer: It goes on a card or loan, where interest and fees keep adding to it
questions.explanation: Without a cushion, the emergency is borrowed, and interest and fees make it grow beyond the original bill. With a cushion, it becomes a withdrawal that you then rebuild.

source.quote: When an emergency goes on a card or a loan, the one-time expense can grow well beyond the original bill because of interest and fees. That is how one repair bill can keep costing long after it is paid.

questions.question: What problem can a scheduled transfer from checking to savings cause, and how can you guard against it?
options: Missing an employer match; send the transfer to an IRA instead
Losing principal if the bank fails; move the money into mutual funds
Fees if checking is short that day; check the balance before it runs
Spending the cushion on wants; keep it in the everyday checking account
questions.correctAnswer: Fees if checking is short that day; check the balance before it runs
questions.explanation: An automatic transfer can trigger overdraft fees when checking can't cover it. The chapter says to watch the balance or set a reminder before the transfer runs.

source.quote: An automatic transfer can trigger overdraft fees if checking is short on the day it runs. Keep an eye on the balance, or set a reminder to check it before the transfer runs.

questions.question: How does keeping emergency money apart from investments help when the market falls?
options: It earns enough to outweigh the interest on high interest credit cards
It makes the invested money federally insured against loss of principal
A surprise bill need not be paid by selling investments that have dropped
It lets the investments take on more risk with no chance of any loss
questions.correctAnswer: A surprise bill need not be paid by selling investments that have dropped
questions.explanation: Investments can lose value, and the cushion means you don't have to sell them at a low point to cover a bill. The other options contradict the text: investments aren't insured, all carry risk, and no investment beats card interest for sure.

source.quote: This is the trade the cushion protects. With the emergency money held elsewhere, a bill need not be paid by selling investments after they have fallen.

questions.question: Fund A and Fund B hold the same investments, but Fund A costs 0.2% a year and Fund B costs 1.0% a year. Which should leave you with more money over time, and why?
options: Fund A, because lower yearly costs leave more of the returns
Fund B, because higher charges usually mean better management
Fund B, because managed funds generally charge lower fees
Neither, because small fee gaps even out over the years held
questions.correctAnswer: Fund A, because lower yearly costs leave more of the returns
questions.explanation: When two funds are alike except for their charges, the cheaper one leaves you more money. Small fees add up over the years.

source.quote: Of two funds alike in every way except their charges, the one with lower annual costs leaves you with more money.
